title: Financial plan structure, assumptions and break-even for pool service work
audience: Owners who prepare the financial section of a pool service plan
learningOutcomes: Describe the parts of a financial plan for pool service work: forecast, profit and loss, cash flow, balance sheet and break-even
Write an assumptions register that links volume, price and cost for each forecast line
Work out a break-even point in words and with the business's own inputs
Identify the financing needs and state each one with its basis

instruction.heading: The parts of the finance section
instruction.body: A financial plan for pool service work usually contains a sales forecast, a income and expense statement, a cash flow statement, a balance sheet, a break-even analysis and a statement of financing needs. The sample plan has all of these as blank tables with zero entries, so it shows the structure only. The business's numbers must come from its own volumes, prices and costs, with the assumptions written down.

instruction.heading: The assumptions register
instruction.body: Every forecast line rests on an assumption. For a pool business the main ones are the number of visits per week, the number of clients on each service, the average price per visit, the chemical and supply cost per visit, the travel time and cost, the labour cost, the insurance cost, the vehicle and equipment cost, the overheads and the owner's pay. Write each assumption, its value, its basis and its date. The method is taught in “Writing the assumptions register behind a projection”.

instruction.heading: Profit, cash and the balance sheet
instruction.body: The income and expense statement shows the income and costs over a period. The cash flow statement shows when money comes in and goes out, which can differ widely, because clients pay later than the visit and some costs fall before any income. The balance sheet shows what the business owns and owes at a date. Read these together with “Reading a profit and loss forecast” and “Reading a projected balance sheet”, and check that a profit does not hide a cash shortfall.

instruction.heading: Break-even
instruction.body: The break-even point is the level of activity at which income equals costs. In words: divide the fixed costs for the period by the margin each visit contributes after its direct costs, and that gives the number of visits needed to break even. Use only the business's own fixed costs, margin and assumptions. “Break-even and sales forecast by stage” describes the method for a stage-by-stage break-even. Avoid using a sample plan's break-even table, because its figures are placeholders.

instruction.heading: Financing needs
instruction.body: State the financing needs in two parts: the start-up costs, such as equipment, vehicle, initial supplies and registration fees, and the working capital needed to cover the time before cash comes in. For each need, state the amount it is built from, the source of the funds and the date needed.

procedure: Write the sales forecast from the visit volume and the price for each service.
Build the profit and loss from the forecast, with each cost line linked to an assumption.
Build the cash flow, showing the timing of payments in and out.
Build the balance sheet at the period end, and check it balances.
Work out the break-even in words and with the business's own inputs.
State the financing needs with the basis and the timing for each.
Record every assumption in the register, with its basis and date.

workedExamples.situation: The forecast shows a profit each month, but the cash flow shows the business runs out of money in the third month because clients pay late.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not treat the profit as enough. Add the timing of client payments to the cash flow, and state the working capital needed to bridge the gap. Record the assumption on payment timing and show the financing need it creates.

workedExamples.situation: A break-even figure is copied from the sample plan, which shows a blank table.
workedExamples.reasoning: Avoid using the sample figure. Rebuild the break-even from the business's own fixed costs, margin and visit volume, and record each input in the assumptions register.

equipmentAndPpe: Spreadsheet or the financial forecast template

commonErrors.error: Using the sample plan's numbers or blank table values
commonErrors.prevention: Build every line from the business's own volumes, prices and costs.
Build a cash flow with the payment timing of clients and suppliers.
Record each assumption with its value, basis and date.

commonErrors.error: Omitting tax or insurance costs without a check
commonErrors.prevention: Leave tax and insurance out until they are checked.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Check tax treatment, including any goods and services tax, insurance costs and financing terms with the relevant regulator before relying on this point.
The sample plan's financial tables are blank placeholders. They are not a source of figures.
This lesson gives no financial advice. A suitable adviser should check the forecast before it is relied on for financing.

qualityStandard: Each forecast line has a linked assumption with its basis and date.
The cash flow shows the timing of payments, and the balance sheet balances at each period end.
The break-even uses only the business's own inputs, and each input is recorded.
documentationEvidence: Cash flow and balance sheet for each period
Break-even worksheet and financing needs statement
summary: Every forecast line rests on a recorded assumption.
A profit does not prove cash is available. Build the cash flow with payment timing.
Break-even uses the business's own costs and margin, never a sample table.

knowledgeChecks.question: A forecast shows a profit but the cash flow shows a shortfall. What is the most likely cause?
options: The sample plan has blank tables in the back of the file and the appendix
The balance sheet is wrong about the cash and the debtors at the start
The timing of client payments and supplier payments differs from the profit
The break-even point is too low for the business and the area it serves

knowledgeChecks.question: How should a break-even point be worked out for pool service work?
options: From the competitor's published revenue for the year, the quarter and the month
By doubling the first month's income for the whole year, the season and the quarter
From the sample plan's table of figures, notes, the appendix, the totals and the summary
From the business's own fixed costs and the margin per visit, recorded as assumptions

knowledgeChecks.question: Which is a required element of a pool business's financing needs statement?
options: Each need with its basis, source of funds and timing
A promise that the business will be profitable
The sample plan's loan figures for the new shop
A list of competitors' funding for the year
